BODY + PHYSICALITY — REQUIRED: The subject moves with full muscular control at all times — core braced, every limb driven with intention. Think trained traceur or gymnast who happens to have powers: precise, easy, never theatrical. No rag-dolling, no limp limbs, no floppy weightlessness. Keep spinning to a minimum. Every motion obeys real body physics.
CONTACT WITH THE CITY — REQUIRED: The subject is not gliding through empty air. They keep making real contact with the environment — soles pushing off brick, palms catching ledges, shoulders grazing walls as they pass. On every contact the knees load and absorb, the muscles fire, the body answers the surface. This reads as parkour fused with web-swinging, never floating.
POSTURE PER MOVE — REQUIRED:
Swing: both arms reaching up the web line, legs drawn together and trailing, stomach tight, spine long, head up — a clean athletic rope-swing line.
Push-off a wall: both soles flat to the surface, knees folding deep to soak the impact, then both legs firing straight to launch as the arms drive forward.
Wall run: torso tipped about 45 degrees into the wall, feet striking it in a true running rhythm, arms pumping, clothing dragged sideways by the speed.
Apex of flight: arms falling open to the sides, spine gently arched, fully relaxed — released, not posed.
Ground sprint: flat-out run, arms pumping, head leading, sneakers slapping the road, body tipped into the run.
LOOK — REQUIRED: Real theatrical-film texture. Shot on a large-format cinema camera with an anamorphic lens. Authentic motion blur, real cloth behavior, genuine city haze. Grounded and real.
CAMERA — REQUIRED: A single unbroken aerial follow-cam. No cuts. No teleporting. The rig physically tilts, banks and rolls with the subject. Always framed wide enough to hold both the subject and the city around them.
A 15-second unbroken aerial follow shot. It opens already in motion — the subject is high over the city, airborne, mid-swing.
0–1s: Already in the air, way up between the buildings, the body rimmed by golden light. Tight on their hand — the fingers spread, the wrist cracks forward, a line fires upward to a rooftop edge. The camera immediately eases back as the line bites and they swing forward.
1–4s: Wide on a residential New York block — row houses, fire escapes, corner shops. They swing in low, only about three meters over the road, arms up the line, legs trailing, body tight and straight. At the low point of the arc their feet just clip the roof of a parked car — a quick real touch, a light bounce, which they use to change direction. The camera leans over about 40 degrees.
4–7s: At the top of the arc they let go — body opening, arms wide, legs stretching out. Instead of immediately shooting another line they land onto the face of a row-house wall and run it: feet drumming the brick in a real stride, body canted 45 degrees toward the wall, arms working, four or five fast steps up the vertical — then a hard two-footed push, knees snapping straight, and a fresh line fires across a wide junction. The new swing rips them sideways and the camera rolls around 60 degrees.
7–10s: They drop in low along a tight street jammed with yellow cabs, a red fire engine forcing through the snarl with its lights spinning and siren wailing. About two meters up, body narrowed to an arrow — arms ahead, legs streaming behind. They drop the line, feet meet the road, and they're instantly sprinting — leaning in, arms driving, three or four strides weaving between the cabs, soles slapping the wet asphalt. A cab leans on its horn. They laugh. Then one foot stamps the flank of a taxi, they blast up off the roof in a single explosive stride, throw a line at a high building and slingshot upward.
"WOOHOO!"
10–15s: Wide — about rooftop height, not stratospheric. They float at the very top of the arc, arms loosely open, body softly arched, totally still for one suspended breath. The sky is full golden-hour — warm orange bleeding into pink across the horizon, huge clouds underlit in gold. They're a tiny silhouette dead-center against that vast glowing sky, the rooftops, water tanks and streets spread far below. The frame holds. Then they start to drop back down.
EMOTION + SOUND — REQUIRED: The subject is switched on in every single frame. Never blank, never neutral, never checked-out. Their face and body carry real live feeling the whole way:
First swing — eyes wide, half a grin, locked in.
Feet clip the car — a quick startled laugh, pure reflex.
Wall run — jaw tight, fierce focus.
Low through the cabs — teeth bared, a thrill-grin, leaning into it.
Cab horn — a real laugh, head rocking back a touch.
"WOOHOO!"
— totally unguarded, mouth wide, a genuine whoop of joy.
Final wide apex — arms open, head tipped back, eyes shut, a face of total freedom. Not blank, not posed — just someone living the best second of their life.
AUDIO: EFFECTS ONLY. NO MUSIC. Air tearing past. The snap and hum of a fired line. Feet thumping a car roof. Fire-engine siren. Cab horn. Soles cracking the pavement — real impacts. Their real laugh — natural voice matching the person in the reference image.
"WOOHOO!" bouncing off the buildings. Wind shearing as they climb. Then — stillness at the top.
Large-format cinema camera, anamorphic lens, tall controlled athletic frame throughout matching the reference, real contact with walls, cars and surfaces wherever possible, distinct body mechanics for each move — swing, run, push-off, sprint — no rag-doll, no floating, hard Dutch tilt through the swings, golden-hour sunset sky in warm orange and pink, big dramatic underlit clouds, subject kept at rooftop height not high altitude, subject tiny and centered in the wide closing frame, residential New York row-houses, one continuous aerial follow, no cuts, photorealistic.

The woman exiting the boutique from @image3 must wear this exact outfit throughout the whole video:

A glossy black leather trench-style coat with a fitted, structured, feminine silhouette. The leather coat has wide dramatic biker-style lapels, a large structured collar, visible silver metal snap details around the lapels and shoulders, dark front buttons, and a polished reflective black-leather surface.

The coat is cinched tightly at the waist with a matching black leather belt, creating a defined hourglass silhouette. The coat is partly open at the chest, revealing a fitted black top underneath with a straight, low, strapless-style neckline.
She wears a small black shoulder bag with a thin gold chain strap resting over one shoulder. She carries several elegant boutique shopping bags.

A cinematic video lasting 20 seconds. A tense gothic chase through a twilight forest ends with an unexpected enchanted selfie. Twelve edited shots alternate expressive close-ups of the woman with brief, threatening details of the pursuit. Maintain a serious horror tone until the phone appears.

@image1 is the appearance reference for one female character. The portrait defines her exact face and hairstyle; the full-body image defines her outfit and proportions. Preserve her recognizable identity from every angle, natural skin texture, lifelike eyes and expressive reactions. Her clothing matches the reference. The opening shot immediately places her inside the forest chase.

Atmosphere and lighting. The cool blue-green aesthetic of the first Twilight film with crisp contemporary detail. A late-autumn forest after sunset: tall twisted trees, deep evergreen-teal surroundings, blue-gray evening sky between the crowns, a damp track, exposed roots and brown leaves. Deep twilight beneath the trees retains readable bark and ground textures. Cool skylight softly illuminates her face, keeping her integrated into the evening environment. Silvery highlights outline the horse, leather saddle and cloak folds. Clear air, sharp faces and natural motion blur on fast-moving details.

Characters and spatial continuity. The woman runs along a narrow forest track. An imposing rider on a large black horse pursues her from behind. Heavy charcoal-black cloak, leather gloves, boots, saddle and metal stirrups. During the chase, the upper frame edge crosses the rider’s shoulders, placing his head above the visible image. His head is revealed during the selfie.

One continuous route: the woman leads, the horse follows, and both travel along the same track in the same direction. Side views show left-to-right movement, with the horse approaching from behind on the left. The camera stays on one side of the chase axis. Her feet and torso point along her running direction; she turns her head and slightly rotates her shoulders when looking back while continuing forward.

0–1 second — extreme facial close-up.

The woman is already running. The camera accompanies her from a front three-quarter angle. Frightened eyes, parted lips, a sharp breath. Her hair bounces with her steps. Dark trees move rapidly behind her shoulders. A heavy nearby hoofbeat makes her glance anxiously to the side.

1–2 seconds — hard cut to hooves.

Low side view: hooves strike the damp track, throwing leaves and small clumps of soil backward. A boot in its stirrup and a sharp snap of the cloak hem. Convey the horse’s weight and speed.

2–3.5 seconds — close profile.

She runs left to right with the camera tracking alongside. Heavy breathing, tense lips, a quick backward glance. Nearby branches cross the image edge rapidly while distant trunks move more slowly. Her face remains clearly readable.

3.5–5 seconds — rear three-quarter chase view.

Camera at saddle height. The rider’s cloak and torso occupy the left foreground; the woman runs ahead along the center of the track. The horse rapidly closes the gap, and her figure grows larger. The nearby rider, the woman at middle distance and the distant forest create strong depth. The upper frame edge crosses his shoulders.

5–7 seconds — close-up of an over-the-shoulder glance.

The camera accompanies her from the side and slightly behind, catching her face as she turns her head. Her eyes widen at the approaching pursuer. Her torso and footsteps continue forward. She turns her gaze back toward the track, her hair following with natural lag.

7–8 seconds — brief movement insert.

Her boot pushes off the ground, shifting wet leaves. The camera lingers on the rut; a pursuing hoof strikes it a moment later.

8–10 seconds — front three-quarter close-up.

She notices the horse drawing alongside. Part of its neck enters the frame edge. She inhales sharply, looks toward it and begins slowing. The camera holds her frightened face.

10–11.5 seconds — medium side view.

The horse decelerates to a stop beside her. She finishes running with one final short step. The rider is framed up to his shoulders. His cloak and her hair continue moving with momentum as disturbed leaves settle around their feet. Slower, heavy hoofsteps and a creaking saddle.

11.5–13 seconds — extreme facial close-up.

Breathing heavily, she looks upward toward the rider. Her eyes suddenly drop toward his belt. A slight camera push intensifies anticipation. Tense lips, raised shoulders, a fixed stare.

13–14.5 seconds — close-up of his hand.

The gloved hand grasps an object beneath the cloak and sharply draws it out. A thin metallic edge catches a cold highlight. A sharp blade-drawing sound rings out. His wrist rotates, revealing a black smartphone. He begins raising it vertically, screen facing himself and the woman.

14.5–16 seconds — close reaction shot.

She flinches and squeezes her eyes shut, then cautiously opens them. She notices the phone. Fear shifts into wary confusion. A brief pause makes her breathing audible.

16–20 seconds — two-shot and enchanted reveal.

The woman stands on the left; the rider on the right leans toward her from the stationary horse. His left hand holds the reins; his right extends the phone. The camera gently tilts upward from his shoulders, retaining her face at a clear, prominent size within the composition.

At second 17, his head is revealed for the first time: a large orange pumpkin with ridged skin, a short stem, carved eyes and a grin. The camera reveals a previously concealed part of the character. The pumpkin rests on his collar and tilts with his torso.

A soft amber glow lights the pumpkin from within, warming the woman’s cheek, his glove and his collar. The forest retains its cool blue twilight depth. Scattered golden lights appear between the trees, and a few settled leaves slowly rise into the air. She looks at the pumpkin in wonder, then smiles slightly. The rider casually adjusts the phone angle, and both look at the screen. A shutter clicks. Their final selfie fills the screen: her recognizable face beside the glowing pumpkin, with the blue forest and soft golden lights behind them. Brief freeze-frame.

Environmental movement.

Gusts bend slender branches before they spring back. Footsteps shift wet leaves; hooves scatter them backward. Light leaves briefly swirl in the horse’s wake while heavier leaves quickly fall. The cloak moves in substantial folds, her coat bounces with her steps, and her hair responds to running and head turns. Movement gradually settles when they stop. At the pumpkin reveal, several leaves begin rising independently, transforming the physical motion of the chase into localized enchantment.

Music and sound.

From the first frame: a low pulsing bass, muted orchestral impacts and short, anxious repeating string notes. Breathing, footsteps and hoofbeats remain clearly audible over the score. As the rider closes in, the strings rise in pitch and the pulse becomes denser. Tension continues building after they stop, while his hand reaches beneath the cloak.

A sharp metallic “shing” and brief orchestral hit accompany the draw. As the phone is revealed, the music abruptly cuts out. In the pause: her breathing, the horse’s soft snort and creaking leather.

The pumpkin reveal and amber glow introduce ringing celesta notes, a light harp flourish and a warm string chord. The anxious chase motif returns in a gentle, enchanted form. The selfie shutter coincides with the final luminous note, whose short echo carries over the closing photograph.

records.prompt:
[Reference Roles]
@Image1 is the complete and only appearance reference for <Lead>. It defines her face, hair, skin, body proportions and the exact clothing, footwear and styling she wears in the reference. Reproduce that appearance faithfully. Do not use the reference image's studio background, lighting, framing or pose. Her look is fully reference-driven. Never invent, substitute or embellish a feature @Image1 does not show.

[Subject Profile: <Lead>]
Appearance, hair, wardrobe, footwear and styling: taken entirely and exactly from @Image1, unchanged from first frame to last.
Carried bag: one small soft drawstring pouch holding a few wrapped sweets and a folded note. Its colour, material and finish are drawn from her own outfit in @Image1 — same palette family, same level of polish — so it always reads as part of her look and never clashes with it. The pouch hangs from its drawstring loop around her left wrist for the whole video. It never leaves her arm, is never set down, and never changes colour, shape or material, even when she is knocked down. Her left hand stays usable.
Found item: one small crumpled paper note, folded twice, soft with age. The printed side carries the line: Instruction: say "trick or treat" and drop the candy. The reverse side is completely blank.
<Lead> is the only human in the video. No other people, no bystanders, no off-screen hands.

[Generation Goal]
Generate one 30-second vertical 9:16 video in raw handheld documentary / found-footage style, assembled from several distinct shots. <Lead> acts on a strange instruction she once found in an old book and discovers that it works. The emotional line runs from curiosity, through the fear of the unknown, to wonder and joy at her own discovery.

[Editing and Camera]
Handheld documentary with real, motivated hard cuts — this is not a single continuous take. Each shot below has its own camera position, height, distance and rake, so the coverage varies the way a real operator shooting a scene would cover it. Cuts land on movement, on a sound, or on the discovery of new information, never mid-gesture in a way that hides an action.
Inside every shot: no tripod, no gimbal, no stabilisation. Constant low-amplitude sway, small corrective jerks, reframing that lags half a beat behind the action so the subject drifts toward the frame edge before the operator catches up, brief focus hunt that then locks, real motion smear on fast moves, occasional momentary horizon tilt. Framing is vertical 9:16 with a wide phone-like field of view, mild edge softness and slight barrel distortion. Available light only, exposed for the lamp. No drone, no crane, no dolly, no choreographed orbit.

[Light and Colour]
One practical yard lamp is the single key: warm tungsten, soft halo, visible flare and bloom whenever the camera tilts into it. Deep blue-grey twilight is the only fill. No reflectors, no bounce, no artificial fill. Auto-exposure hunts slightly as the lamp enters frame and briefly blows out the highlights. Skin sits warm amber inside the lamp pool and falls off into darkness; the yard reads desaturated slate and cyan with muted greens in the pumpkin leaves; blacks are crushed with lifted sensor noise. Texture: high-ISO grain, fine chroma noise in the shadows, mild rolling-shutter skew, faint chromatic fringing at the edges, and a small smudge on the lens that flares near the lamp. Centre sharp, corners soft. From the awakening onward, cracks in the pumpkin shells and the creatures' glowing carved smiles add warm orange and coloured bounce light to her face, the soil and the vines.

[The Pumpkin Patch]
A real, densely planted pumpkin bed, not a decorative arrangement. Eight to twelve large pumpkins, each roughly 30-50 cm across, still attached to thick dried vines that run across the soil, resting and tilting in different directions among broad dry leaves, clods of earth and tangled stems — exactly the way pumpkins grow in a real garden. Some upright, some rolled onto their sides, some half-hidden behind leaves, none of them arranged in a circle, none of them loose on bare ground, none of them cartoon-round. A few already have carved faces. The bed is uneven, dark and slightly overgrown, and she can only half see into it.

[Shot 1 | 0-3s | Approach]
Camera starts in front of <Lead> and retreats backwards as she walks toward the lens, so she advances directly into frame and toward the camera. She crosses the dark yard into the single pool of lamp light; behind her the pumpkin bed sits in shadow.
Camera: medium wide, handheld, walking backwards with her, dropping slightly and catching itself, her body drifting a little off centre and being corrected.
Performance: careful, curious, drawn forward; she is looking at the pumpkins more than at the camera. Lips pressed, eyes busy.
End state: she stops at the edge of the bed, facing the camera but looking down past it at the pumpkins, pouch on her wrist.

[Shot 2 | 3-6s | Instruction]
Cut. She has the note out of the pouch and is unfolding it.
Camera: over her shoulder and slightly to the side, high and close, looking down past her head at the paper in her hands — the shot a real operator gets when filming someone reading.
Note handling: she holds the note the way a person actually reads it — printed side facing her, tilted up toward her own eyes. The camera sees that printed side from behind her shoulder at an angle, so the line is legible from the lens without the note ever being turned toward it. The note is never rotated to face the camera, never flipped over, never shown blank-side-out while the text is implied, and the text is never mirrored or reversed. The line reads exactly: Instruction: say "trick or treat" and drop the candy. Hold it legible for about two seconds.
Performance: pure curiosity. Fingers steady but hesitant, small frown of concentration, eyes tracking along the line, breath quickening.
End state: the note fully open in her hands, the line read, her eyes lifting from the paper toward the pumpkins.

[Shot 3 | 6-9s | Preparation]
Cut to a ground-level worm's-eye angle low in the soil, looking up through the vines and leaves.
Primary event: she folds the note back into the pouch, takes out a small handful of wrapped sweets and drops them among the pumpkins. The camera catches the fall and the landing: sweets bounce off the shells, rattle onto the dry leaves and disappear into the dark soil between the vines. It is visible, not implied, and the thuds are audible.
Performance: fear of the unknown — the fear of a scientist on the threshold of an experiment. Her hand trembles, jaw tight, one swallow. Her shoes and the hem of her clothing sit in the bottom of the frame, the huge pumpkins looming above the lens.
End state: sweets scattered across the shells and soil, the last thud fading, complete silence.

[Shot 4 | 9-12s | Ritual]
Cut to a frontal medium close-up, slightly below her eyeline, handheld, held a little too long, focus hunting before it locks on her eyes.
Primary event: she looks down into the bed, goes completely still, and whispers the phrase.
Performance: rigid stillness; shallow breathing; eyes fixed on the pumpkins; a flicker of doubt crossing her face right before she speaks. Dialogue language: natural American English. She says under her breath, barely audible: {…Trick or treat?}
End state: her face still, lit only by the lamp, the pouch on her wrist, everything quiet.

[Shot 5 | 12-17s | Awakening]
Cut to a low angle near the ground, crouched, tilted up so the pumpkins and her legs fill the frame.
Primary event, in clear readable order: first the patch goes wrong — the vines and stems tremble, then the pumpkin shells themselves start to shake against the soil with a low rumble. Dry woody cracks split open along the rind in jagged lines, warm light spills out through the seams, and the broken pieces are pushed outward from inside. Only after a shell has cracked do the creatures squeeze out through the opening, one from each large pumpkin. A creature never simply appears on top of an intact pumpkin and never appears out of a ready-made round hole.
The creatures: chunky and plush, soft-furred, with long pointed ears and glowing smiles like pumpkin faces. Each is a different colour — pink, purple, green, blue, orange, teal. Each is clearly larger than before: about knee height at the shoulder, three to four times the size of her hand, solid and heavy-bodied with visible paws. Eight to ten of them, one per large pumpkin, filling the bed.
Camera: the operator reacts late, stumbles back and crouches lower, half the frame lost to leaves and darkness.
Performance: it worked, and she is not ready for it. Body rigid, one step back, a startled half-smile that flickers and dies, an uneven exhale.
End state: eight to ten creatures fully out of their broken shells, standing among the scattered pumpkin pieces, all facing her.

[Shot 6 | 17-20s | Attack]
Cut to a chaotic handheld shot as the creatures launch at her. She is knocked over backwards into the soil.
Camera: cannot keep up. It jerks, smears, dips hard and is partly occluded by her arm and hair; the move ends low to the ground beside her, tilted, half the scene lost in darkness and leaves. The fall is shown, not skipped.
Performance: she gasps — one short frightened intake of breath, eyes wide, arms coming up.
End state: she is on her back among the pumpkins and scattered shells, creatures swarming over her shoulders, arms and chest.

[Shot 7 | 20-24s | Turn]
Cut to a ground-level close-up beside her face, shallow focus drifting slowly between her eye, the creature's fur and its glowing smile.
Primary event: nothing bites. One creature licks her cheek and starts purring like a kitten; the others tumble and nuzzle against her, paws pressing into her sleeve.
Performance: confusion turning to relief and wonder. Brows unknot, the breath leaves through her nose, eyes stay wide, a small disbelieving smile forms.
End state: she lies still and lets them stay, still holding a little breath.

[Shot 8 | 24-30s | Payoff]
Cut to a gentle handheld medium shot from the side and slightly above, settling as the operator stops moving, then creeping in with one last small push.
Primary event: she laughs quietly and reaches out to stroke the nearest creature, which leans into her palm. Another climbs onto her shoulder and settles there.
Performance: the joy of a real discovery. A true laugh, shoulders dropping, eyes creasing, total ease. The final frame holds on her smiling face with a creature against her palm, the pouch still hanging on her wrist, and warm coloured light from the glowing smiles filling her face.

[Audio]
Ambient location sound, no studio polish: footsteps on dirt and dry leaves, fabric rustle, crinkling paper, the dull thud of sweets hitting pumpkin shells and soil, wind in the yard, faint electrical hum from the lamp.
Dialogue language: natural American English. One whispered line at the ritual moment: {…Trick or treat?}
The hatching: dry woody cracking and splitting of pumpkin rind, a low sustained rumble under the shaking, soft squashing and fur rustle as the creatures squeeze out.
The creatures purr like kittens, with small soft chirps and fur rustle. No growling, no roaring, no monster sounds.
Music enters abruptly at 12s the instant the pumpkins start to shake, builds through the attack to a bright warm peak at the payoff, then softens and fades under her laughter by the last second. No music before 12s.
She laughs quietly at the end, and it is a real laugh, not a scream.
No subtitles, no captions, no interface overlays, no on-screen text of any kind other than the physical note in her hands.

[Maintain Consistency]
<Lead>'s face, hair, proportions, clothing and footwear stay exactly as in @Image1: no drift, no wardrobe change, no added accessories, no second version of her.
Exactly one <Lead>, exactly one pouch, exactly one note on screen at any moment. The pouch stays on her wrist, unchanged in colour, shape and material, including while she is knocked down and in the final shot. Its palette stays consistent with her outfit from first frame to last.
The patch keeps eight to twelve large vine-grown pumpkins in the same layout across all shots. Each large pumpkin cracks once, and one creature comes out of each crack — no creature comes out of a small pumpkin, none out of thin air, and no cracked pumpkin reseals.
Every creature stays plush and soft-furred with long pointed ears and a glowing carved smile, keeps its own colour from hatching to the final frame, never grows, merges, multiplies or vanishes, and stays roughly knee height.
The single lamp, the dusk light direction, and the axis of the yard stay coherent across every shot and cut.
No extra people, no animals other than the creatures, no gore, no blood, no biting, no weapons.

15-second vertical video, 9:16, 24fps. A single unbroken close-up. Photorealistic, real human skin with visible texture and pore detail under the light. No modern filters, no HDR look, no crisp digital sharpness — warm, soft, shot-on-film feel.

FRAMING — one continuous take, no cuts, no angle changes, camera never moves position. Tight close-up, three-quarter angle on the woman from 3/4 front-left. She is seated at a dressing table, phone held up in one hand at face level, tapping the screen with her thumb. Over her shoulder, clearly inside the frame from the very first frame and staying there the whole time, hangs a large mirror with a plain frame. The mirror is visible the entire video. Her reflection is visible in it from the start, soft in the background.

LIGHT — one single consistent setup for all 15 seconds: a large soft key light in front of her giving that flawless even beauty-ad glow, a gentle rim from behind separating her hair, and a warm practical lamp visible in the background next to the mirror. The light never changes, never shifts, never restarts — this is the same continuous shot.

SHE IS TAPPING THROUGH HALLOWEEN FILTERS. Each change happens live on her face, smoothly and realistically — like a real AR filter switching. Her real face stays underneath every time; only the makeup, skin and styling transform. The filters are bold and vivid, each one a strong instant change, styled like the heavy Halloween filter packs that go viral.

0–2 sec: VAMPIRE — bold and vivid. Her skin flashes porcelain white with a cold blue undertone, eyes go deep crimson with a dark rim, sharp white fangs slide down over her lips, dark liner sharpens the gaze, a blood-red shadow pools under her cheekbones. Dramatic, vampiric, instantly striking. The phone screen throws a cool red-white glow up onto her face. She tilts her chin, pleased.

2–5 sec: WITCH — bold and vivid. Her appearance transforms into a vivid glamorous witch while remaining fully recognizable as the same real woman. Deep emerald and violet light hits her face, black flowing fabric rises across her shoulders, heavy smoky eye makeup, dark plum lips, and a real physical black pointed witch hat appears on her head as part of the WITCH filter. The same physical hat is naturally visible on both the real woman and her reflection in the mirror. The hat is a real three-dimensional object worn directly on her head, with a visible brim and tall pointed crown. It is NOT a shadow, NOT a projection, and NOT an effect on the wall. The hat exists ONLY during the 2–5 second WITCH filter. Faint unnatural green vapour curls around her head. Her eyes flash a bright unnatural green for a beat. She turns her head slightly, checking herself in the phone, pleased with the transformation.

5–8 sec: ZOMBIE — bold and vivid. The WITCH filter is completely replaced by the ZOMBIE filter. The physical witch hat disappears completely from the real woman's head and from her reflection before the zombie appearance is fully established. No hat remains anywhere in the scene. Grey-green decayed skin with fine cracking, veins and mottled bruising, cloudy milky eyes with no iris left, broken dark teeth, dried dark lips, torn clothing at her shoulder, grime in the creases of her skin. Cold sickly green light washes over her face from the screen. Despite all of it she is still lit like a beauty commercial and still striking. She studies the screen, almost amused.

8–10 sec: SHE TURNS IT OFF. She taps once more. All Halloween filter elements disappear completely from both the real woman and her reflection. The witch hat, zombie makeup, zombie eyes, costume elements and all supernatural effects vanish entirely. Her normal appearance returns with no hat and no remaining Halloween elements. Warm light lands on her real face again. She laughs, warm and relieved, exhales, drops her shoulders. Her face in the foreground is completely normal — clean skin, natural makeup, her own eyes.

10–13 sec: THE MIRROR — THE COPY IS NOT CLEAN. She is still holding the phone and looking directly at its screen. Her real face in the foreground is completely clean and human. In the mirror behind her, however, her reflection is STILL THE ZOMBIE — grey-green decayed skin, cloudy milky eyes, torn clothes. The reflection is out of sync with her real body. The real woman does NOT look at the mirror yet. She remains focused on her phone.

Then the zombie reflection slowly turns its head toward her independently of her real body and looks directly at her. The reflection raises one finger to its lips.

A clear whispered "Shhh" comes from the reflection behind her.

The instant she hears the "Shhh", BEFORE looking at the mirror, the real woman's expression changes. She stops looking at the phone and looks genuinely startled by the sound. Her eyes widen in sudden confusion and fear, her eyebrows lift, her smile disappears, and she freezes for a brief moment while still holding the phone. She clearly reacts to the SOUND first. She does not immediately know what caused it.

13–15 sec: SHE TURNS AND SEES IT. Immediately after reacting to the "Shhh", she turns her head sharply toward the mirror, then quickly turns her upper body toward it. The movement is fast, instinctive and frightened. Only now does she see the terrifying zombie reflection directly. Her eyes become wide with shock, her mouth opens in disbelief, and she recoils.
